definition: enhanced oscillation of a system driven periodically at a frequency near one of its natural frequencies
the rate of flow of electric charge through a surface or past a point
the change in electric potential energy per unit charge between two points; measured in volts (joules per coulomb)

the expected number of radioactive decays per unit time in a sample; also called decay rate
the component of a contact force perpendicular to the surface of contact
a decrease in electric potential across a circuit component, corresponding to a decrease in electric potential energy per unit positive charge

a conducting enclosure that shields its interior from external electrostatic fields
a steady distribution of charge with no net macroscopic flow of charge
the addition of individual wave disturbances to obtain the resulting disturbance where waves overlap, for waves obeying the superposition principle
frequencies of vibration above the fundamental frequency; when they are integer multiples of the fundamental, they are also harmonics
reinforcement where overlapping wave disturbances add in the same direction
partial or complete cancellation where overlapping wave disturbances have opposite directions
units of the International System of Units, including base units such as the metre, kilogram, and second, and derived units such as the newton and joule
base units chosen for a system of quantities; other units are formed from combinations of these units
a system of measurement using decimal multiples and submultiples of units; SI is its modern international form
the mass of an atom, including the effects of the binding of its constituents; it is less than the sum of the masses of its separated protons, neutrons, and electrons
the energy released or required in a nuclear reaction, determined by the difference between the total initial and final rest energies
composite particles whose constituents are bound by the strong interaction
elementary particles that do not participate in the strong interaction, including electrons, muons, taus, neutrinos, and their antiparticles
the antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass and a positive electric charge; also called an antielectron
the electrically neutral lepton of electron flavor, associated with the electron in weak interactions
an electrically neutral elementary lepton that participates in the weak interaction; neutrinos occur in electron, muon, and tau flavors
another name for the positron, the electron’s antiparticle
an electron or positron emitted in nuclear beta decay
spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus into a different nucleus or a lower-energy nuclear state
a spontaneous transformation of an unstable particle or nucleus; nuclear decay produces a different nucleus or a lower-energy nuclear state
a nuclear transition to a lower-energy state by emission of a gamma-ray photon, without changing the numbers of protons or neutrons
materials that emit brief flashes of light when they absorb energy from ionizing radiation
a gas-filled radiation detector in which ionizing radiation triggers an electrical discharge that can be registered as a count
a device that registers radiation through its interaction with matter
the greater time interval measured in an inertial frame between ticks of a clock moving relative to that frame, compared with the interval measured by that clock
the time interval measured by a clock present at both events; for an inertial clock, the events occur at the same position in its rest frame

a nonnegative measure of separation or path length; the distance between two positions is their straight-line separation, whereas distance traveled is the total path length
the horizontal distance traveled by a projectile from launch to landing
the path followed by a moving object
a change in an object’s position over time relative to a chosen reference frame

the inward component of the net force responsible for the curvature of an object’s path; for uniform circular motion, it is the entire net force
a change in an object’s shape or size
a force directed toward a stable equilibrium position when a system is displaced from it
a measure of a spring’s stiffness: the ratio of restoring-force magnitude to displacement within the range where Hooke’s law applies
a contact force parallel to a surface that opposes the tendency of surfaces to slip relative to one another while they remain at rest relative to each other
normal force per unit area on a surface
the net upward force due to the pressure of a fluid at rest on an immersed object

for steady, incompressible flow with negligible viscosity along a streamline at constant height, pressure is lower where speed is higher
the energy per unit mass required to change a substance directly from solid to vapor at specified conditions
the energy transferred per unit mass during a specified phase transition at given temperature and pressure
the heat transferred per unit mass per unit temperature change, without a phase change and under specified conditions such as constant pressure or constant volume
a thermodynamic process that occurs at constant pressure
an ideal process that can be reversed so that both the system and its surroundings return to their original states
a physical quantity assigned to each point in space, and possibly time; a vector field also assigns a direction
an idealized electric charge concentrated at a point; a useful model when the charged object’s size is negligible for the problem
a small charge used to probe an electric field, small enough that its effect on the source charges can be neglected
a property of matter that determines its electric interactions; charge can be positive or negative

an elementary particle with negative electric charge; electrons are constituents of atoms and can also exist freely
the temperature above which a ferromagnetic material loses its spontaneous magnetization; it can still respond to an applied magnetic field
the magnetic constant relating currents and magnetic fields in vacuum; approximately 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup> T·m/A
an induced current flows in a direction whose magnetic field opposes the change in magnetic flux that induces it
a voltage that periodically reverses polarity; a sinusoidal voltage is a common example
an electric current that periodically reverses direction; a sinusoidal current is a common example
the dependence of a wave’s propagation speed in a medium on frequency; for light, it can cause different colors to refract through different angles
the point where rays initially parallel to the principal axis converge, or from which they appear to diverge, in the ideal lens or mirror approximation
the signed distance from the center of a thin lens, or the vertex of a mirror, to its principal focal point

a lens that causes rays parallel to its principal axis to spread out as if from a focal point; a concave lens in air is a common example
a concave mirror that brings rays close and parallel to its principal axis toward a focus
an image formed where light rays from each object point actually converge; it can be recorded on a screen placed there
an image at the apparent origin of diverging rays; the rays do not actually converge at the image location
the probability per unit time that an undecayed nucleus will decay; the constant determining the exponential decay rate
a unit of activity equal to exactly 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> becquerels (decays per second), originally based on the activity of one gram of radium-226
a preparation containing a radionuclide and used for medical diagnosis or treatment
the daughter nuclei produced when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission
a model that treats a nucleus as a drop of nuclear matter to describe collective properties such as binding and deformation
protons and neutrons, the constituents of atomic nuclei
an electrically neutral particle found in atomic nuclei; a free neutron is unstable and undergoes beta decay
a quantum number equal to +1 for baryons, −1 for antibaryons, and zero for mesons and leptons; in the quark model, one third of the number of quarks minus antiquarks
the rule that total baryon number remains unchanged in a reaction or decay; no violation has been observed
the SI unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second
a wave pattern with fixed nodes and antinodes, produced by interference of waves traveling in opposite directions
